name: Castor oil
lead: Castor oil is a thick, pale vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of the castor plant, Ricinus communis. About 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleates [1]. It has been used for centuries as a laxative and today also serves as an industrial raw material and cosmetic ingredient [1][8].

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly as a topical oil applied to hair, eyebrows and eyelashes, where proponents say it thickens growth. The Wikipedia article on castor oil makes no hair claims, and no clinical trial of castor oil for hair growth appears in the sources reviewed [1].
Its established medical use is oral, as a stimulant laxative; the US label for an over-the-counter product lists temporary relief of occasional constipation [3].
infobox: Laxative, emollient, industrial lubricant and polymer feedstock [1]
Sold over the counter as a laxative and cosmetic ingredient (US)

paras: Castor oil is recorded as a laxative in the Ebers Papyrus, dated about 1550 BC [1]. Industrially it goes into polyurethanes, coatings, lubricants and biodiesel, and food-grade forms appear as additives [1][8]. It is also a vehicle for some injected medicines [1]. For labour induction, a systematic review of three trials (233 women) reported insufficient evidence of benefit, and all women taking it orally felt nauseous [1].

Cosmetically it acts as an emollient and carrier in products such as lipsticks and hair conditioners [2]. Wikipedia's overview of hair conditioners notes that natural oils have been used to condition hair for centuries, and that modern products have largely replaced simple oils with silicones, fatty alcohols and polymers [7]. Castor oil is not named in that overview [7]. Online, people apply it to scalp, beard, brows and lashes, usually with a brush or fingers.

Taken by mouth, castor oil commonly causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and medical guidance discourages its use for simple constipation [1]. The US label advises against use when abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting are present unless directed by a doctor [3]. Castor beans contain ricin, but ricin is not present in the processed oil [1][2]. A pregnancy drug reference advises against oral or topical use in women who are pre-term pregnant [1].

Seeds contain roughly 30 to 60 percent oil depending on source, and the oil is obtained by pressing or solvent extraction [1][2]. Its distinctive hydroxylated fatty acid, ricinoleic acid, gives it high viscosity and lubricity [2][8]. India is the largest producer [2].

On looksmax.org, castor oil is most often discussed for eyebrows and eyelashes, sometimes combined with rosemary oil, minoxidil or derma stamping. Reports are mixed: one user described a month of nightly use followed by visibly longer lashes and a friend noticing thicker brows [6], while others report barely noticeable changes after a year [4]. A third thread acknowledges no strong evidence while suggesting it may at least coat brows like mascara [5]. Users also describe its thickness as awkward to apply [6].

No studies found. Registered clinical trials listed for castor oil concern labour induction and dental pulp response, not hair or lash growth. Wikipedia's overview of hair conditioners reports no hair-growth evidence for castor oil [7].

timeline.event: Ebers Papyrus records castor oil as a laxative. [1]

lore.intro: Castor oil appears repeatedly in hair, brow and lash threads on looksmax.org as a cheap topical growth aid, often debated as to whether it is effective or 'cope'. [4][5]

claims.claim: Castor oil thickens brows and lengthens lashes.
claims.believers: Some users report noticeable lash growth after about a month of nightly application, and a friend noticing thicker brows. [6]
claims.experts: No published trial in the sources reviewed has tested castor oil for brow or lash growth. [1]

claims.claim: Castor oil barely works compared with other options.
claims.believers: Other users say a year of use, even with minoxidil on brows, produced barely noticeable change, and that a prescription lash product did more. [4]
claims.experts: No trials compare castor oil against these treatments in the sources reviewed. [1]

claims.claim: It is harmless even if the effect is unproven, since it coats hair like mascara.
claims.believers: One user says there is no strong evidence it works but it does no harm and acts like mascara. [5]
claims.experts: Topical safety data for castor oil on hair are not described in the sources reviewed; the label warnings concern oral use. [3]

card.summary: A thick pressed seed oil people rub on hair, brows and lashes; established as a laxative, untested for growth.
card.note: Oral use causes cramping and diarrhoea; no hair-growth trials found.

quick.overview:
Castor oil is a viscous oil pressed from castor beans. It is sold as an over-the-counter laxative and used in cosmetics and industry.

Looksmaxxers apply it to scalp, brows and lashes hoping for thicker growth. Users report mixed results, and no clinical trials on hair growth were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it moisturises and thickens strands. Its main component, ricinoleic acid, makes it very viscous. A hair-growth mechanism has not been shown in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Taken orally it commonly causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and labels advise against use with abdominal pain. A pregnancy reference advises against use in pre-term pregnancy. Ricin from the raw bean is not in the processed oil.
